nodes.rationale: Liveness returns 200 when the process is up and must not check dependencies. Readiness checks DB, Redis, and critical upstreams with short timeouts and returns 503 when not ready.

nodes.label: Automatic Archival Restore
nodes.rationale: Since protocol 23, archived persistent entries in the read-write footprint are restored automatically and storage rent is paid again. Simulation handles this. Temporary entries have no restore path. Code should still use get().unwrap_or(default) or has() where absence matters.

nodes.label: extend_ttl
nodes.rationale: extend_ttl(threshold, extend_to) does nothing unless the current TTL is below the threshold, then sets TTL to extend_to. It is idempotent and never shortens TTL. Extending on write makes active users pay for their own state; extending instance TTL at busy entry points keeps globals alive. Rent is charged at invocation time. No entry can exceed about 180 days (3,110,400 ledgers). A ledger is about 5 seconds (17,280 per day).

nodes.label: Transaction Footprint
nodes.rationale: Every touched ledger entry must be in the footprint whether it is used or not. Each read or write has a fixed cost plus bytes. Minimize distinct entries.

nodes.label: Instance Storage
nodes.rationale: instance() shares one TTL with the contract instance and is archived and restorable with it. Use it for an admin, config, and other small globals. One extend_ttl warms every global, but the entry is capped at 64KB serialized on mainnet. Never put per-user or unbounded data there.

nodes.label: Oracles
nodes.rationale: Enforce freshness bounds, prefer multi-source or median feeds, and add circuit breakers.

nodes.label: Persistent Storage
nodes.rationale: persistent() has a per-key TTL. Expired entries are archived and can be restored. Use it for user balances and anything that must survive. New persistent entries start with about 120 days of TTL on mainnet.

nodes.label: Protocol 23
nodes.rationale: Protocol 23 is when archived persistent entries in the footprint started restoring automatically.

nodes.label: Temporary Storage
nodes.rationale: temporary() has a per-key TTL and is deleted permanently on expiry. Use it for caches, time-bounded data, and oracle prices. It is the cheapest storage, starts around one day of TTL, and has no restore path.

nodes.label: Untrusted Cross-Contract Returns
nodes.rationale: Validate data from other contracts. Allowlist oracles, sanity-check magnitudes, and enforce freshness.

nodes.label: Storage Key Collisions
nodes.rationale: Untyped keys can silently overwrite unrelated data. Always use a #[contracttype] key enum.

nodes.label: TTL and Archival Failures
nodes.rationale: A temporary entry can disappear forever, and a persistent entry can archive. Extend TTLs on hot paths. TTL is not a security control, because anyone can extend an entry with ExtendFootprintTTLOp. Store a deadline in the value and check it.

nodes.label: extend_ttl
nodes.rationale: extend_ttl(threshold, extend_to) extends instance TTL so contract state is not archived.

nodes.label: Storage TTL
nodes.rationale: Storage is rented: every entry has a TTL and can be archived.

nodes.label: Storage TTL Tests
nodes.rationale: get_ttl lives on the testutils storage traits, such as Persistent, and is read inside env.as_contract.

nodes.label: ExtendFootprintTTLOp
nodes.rationale: Anyone can extend any entry's TTL with ExtendFootprintTTLOp and no contract auth. Keep-alive services are possible, and TTL expiry is not a security mechanism. If data must die after a deadline, store the deadline in the value and check it.

nodes.label: Typed Storage Keys
nodes.rationale: A #[contracttype] enum for keys centralizes the schema, prevents collisions, and grows by adding variants. Keep keys fine-grained. Transactions declare a read/write footprint up front and serialize on the same read-write entry, so fine-grained keys let unrelated calls run in parallel. A giant map makes every caller pay to read all of it.

nodes.label: Threat Model
nodes.rationale: Assume the attacker controls every argument, transaction order and timing, every account that does not require a signature, contracts that mimic your interface, and the shape of state they can legally create, including entry counts and TTLs. They can extend your entries' TTLs.

nodes.label: contracterror
nodes.rationale: Returning Result gives callers typed errors. Generated clients expose foo(), which panics on error, and try_foo(), where the inner Err is the contract error and the outer Err is a host failure such as budget, bad auth, or a type mismatch. Use panic_with_error! rather than a bare panic, which surfaces as an opaque host error. Error codes are public ABI and must never be renumbered across upgrades. An Err or panic rolls back all state changes of the invocation, including nested writes.

nodes.label: Env
nodes.rationale: Everything a contract can reach hangs off Env: storage, events, crypto, ledger, deployer, prng, current_contract_address, and invoke_contract. The only clock is env.ledger().timestamp().

nodes.label: Execution Model
nodes.rationale: Contracts run as Wasm guests in a sandboxed host inside stellar-core. A transaction is the atomicity boundary: errors, panics, missing auth, and budget exhaustion roll back every ledger change, including nested writes. A caller can catch a callee error with try_ client methods and continue. Guest code holds host objects by integer handles, and the host meters every step.

nodes.label: env.prng
nodes.rationale: env.prng() is seeded from ledger state and is predictable. Never use it for keys, authorization, or high-stakes randomness.

nodes.label: Reentrancy
nodes.rationale: The host blocks direct and indirect reentrancy on normal calls. External calls are still failure, budget, and side-effect boundaries, so state updates must be ordered deliberately.

nodes.label: No delegatecall
nodes.rationale: Contracts cannot execute foreign bytecode in their own context, so proxy-style delegatecall hijacks do not exist.

nodes.label: No Reentrancy
nodes.rationale: The host blocks reentrant calls, direct or indirect, on normal cross-contract paths. External calls remain failure, budget, and side-effect boundaries, so state updates should still be ordered deliberately.

nodes.label: Env
nodes.rationale: Everything a contract can do hangs off Env. There is no I/O, no networking, and no clock beyond the ledger timestamp.

nodes.label: no_std
nodes.rationale: Contracts must be #![no_std] and use soroban_sdk types such as String, Vec, Map, and Symbol, not the Rust standard library.

nodes.label: Protocol 27
nodes.rationale: This skill was written against protocol 27, which mainnet ran at the time of writing. Live protocol version comes from RPC getVersionInfo or Stellar Lab, not from a frozen doc.

nodes.label: Cross-contract Reentrancy
nodes.rationale: There is no delegatecall, and the host blocks cross-contract reentrancy.

nodes.label: Soroban
nodes.rationale: Smart contracts on Stellar were formerly branded Soroban. The platform name is retired, but the Rust SDK (soroban-sdk) and several tool names keep the prefix.

nodes.label: soroban-sdk
nodes.rationale: The soroban-sdk major version tracks the protocol version. Pin the SDK major to the network you deploy to, because testnet upgrades by validator vote before mainnet. Pre-releases exist only during a protocol rollout and must be pinned with the exact version string.
